topic: Choosing the unit of registration for an AI inventory
stem: In an enterprise AI inventory that downstream risk, assurance and reporting processes all draw on, what should the unit of registration be?

options.text: Each model the organisation has approved for use, with the applications that call it listed beneath it.
Each use case — a defined task, its data, its users and its accountable owner — even where several use cases share one model.
Each vendor contract under which AI capability is procured, with individual deployments recorded as line items against the master agreement.
Each application or repository in the software estate, flagged according to whether it makes calls to a model.

explanation.correct: Every obligation the inventory feeds attaches to a use, not to a technology. Risk tier, data classes touched, whether a human reviews the output, who is accountable, what regulator interest applies — all of these differ between two use cases running on the same model in the same application. Registering by use case means one entry answers the questions the organisation is actually asked. Registering by model or by application forces every downstream consumer to disaggregate the entry before they can use it.

distractors.A: A model-centric register is useful for the platform team managing versions and deprecations, but it cannot carry a risk tier or an accountable owner, because those differ per use. It also makes shared models look like single risks when they are many.
distractors.C: Contract-based registration captures only what was procured. It misses everything built in-house on a general-purpose API, and it groups unrelated uses under one supplier record simply because they were bought together.
distractors.D: Application-level flagging tells you where model calls happen in the codebase, which is a useful engineering view. One application frequently hosts several distinct uses with different data and different oversight, so a single flag cannot express the risk.

explanation.concept: Register AI by use case: a named task, the data it touches, the population it affects, its oversight arrangement and its accountable owner. Models, applications and contracts are attributes of a use case, not the thing being governed.
explanation.tip: When an inventory question offers model, application, contract and use case, pick the one that can carry an owner and a risk tier. Only the use case can.

topic: Amnesty as a route from shadow AI to registered use
stem: An Irish insurance broker with 900 staff ran a discovery exercise and identified more than sixty unsanctioned AI uses, including several where client data was pasted into consumer products. Legal wants disciplinary action against the individuals identified. The broker's stated objective is a complete and accurate AI inventory within six months, and a sanctioned internal gateway went live last month. Which approach best serves that objective?

options.text: Run a time-boxed amnesty with hands-on migration support onto the new gateway, then enforce technically once the migration path is proven — accepting that the sixty identified cases attract no sanction.

Take disciplinary action against the identified individuals and publicise the outcomes internally, so that anyone whose use has not yet been discovered understands the consequence of failing to come forward.
Block the consumer products at the proxy immediately and require a written business case for any exception, working through the resulting requests as they arrive from the affected teams.
Extend the discovery tooling to cover personal devices on the guest network, so the remaining undisclosed uses can be found without depending on anyone choosing to disclose them.

explanation.correct: The objective is a complete inventory, and completeness depends on people volunteering the uses that telemetry cannot see — offline work, personal devices, uses that leave no distinctive spend or traffic signature. The first discovery pass has already established that punishment is available, which is exactly why withholding it buys something: a period in which disclosure is safe. The gateway going live last month is the enabling detail — an amnesty is only credible when there is somewhere for the disclosed use to go, and enforcement afterwards is only fair once a working alternative exists.

distractors.B: Sanctioning the people the exercise found teaches everyone else that being discovered is survivable but disclosing is not. It reliably drives the remaining use onto channels with no telemetry at all, which is the opposite of the stated objective.
distractors.C: Blocking without migration support turns every affected team into an exception request against a process with no capacity to absorb sixty of them. The work does not stop; it moves to whatever route is still open while the queue is worked.
distractors.D: Monitoring personal devices is intrusive, of limited legal comfort in most jurisdictions, and yields little: it finds traffic on the guest network but not what was typed on a phone over cellular. It also destroys the trust that voluntary disclosure depends on.

explanation.concept: Shadow AI converts to governed AI when disclosure is cheaper than concealment. That needs three things at once: a sanctioned destination that actually works, a time-boxed period in which coming forward carries no penalty, and technical enforcement that begins when the period ends.
explanation.tip: Amnesty is only the right answer when the stem establishes that a sanctioned alternative exists. Without one, amnesty just relabels the problem.

topic: Designing a usable disable path for a production AI system
stem: A South African bank's Claude-based collections assistant began sending customers settlement figures calculated on a stale balance. Error rates and latency were normal throughout; a collections supervisor noticed the discrepancy at 22:40 on a Saturday. The documented kill switch is a feature flag held in the platform repository: changing it requires a pull request approved by two platform engineers and a pipeline run that averages twenty-five minutes. Neither approver was reachable and the assistant kept sending for three hours. What should the postmortem require?

options.text: Add a third named approver to the flag repository and extend the platform team's on-call rota to cover weekends, so that two approvals are always obtainable within the response target.
Split flag configuration out of the main deployment into its own lightweight pipeline so the twenty-five minute run drops to under five minutes for a flag-only change.
Make disabling an operational action the on-call engineer can take alone through a documented, audited runbook step with no code review or deployment, and rehearse it on a schedule.
Add an automatic circuit breaker that disables the assistant when the error rate crosses a threshold, so that stopping it does not depend on a human noticing and acting at all.

explanation.correct: A kill switch that runs through code review and a deployment pipeline is not a kill switch; it is a change request with an urgent label. The three-hour delay came from the approval dependency, not from pipeline duration, and shaving minutes off a process that was blocked on unreachable humans changes nothing. Stopping a system must be a unilateral operational action available to whoever is on call, with the audit trail produced after the fact rather than as a precondition. Rehearsing it matters because an untested disable path is discovered to be broken during the incident it was built for.

distractors.A: This keeps the structural dependency and adds redundancy to it. Two approvals from a rota still fail when both are in the same outage, at the same event, or simply asleep — and it holds the bank's ability to stop customer harm hostage to another team's availability.
distractors.B: Pipeline duration was not the binding constraint. Twenty-five minutes was never the problem in a three-hour incident; the assistant kept running because nobody with authority to approve the change could be found.
distractors.D: A circuit breaker is a sound complement but would not have fired here: the stem states error rates and latency were normal. The failure was semantically wrong output that only a human with domain knowledge recognised, which is precisely the case automated thresholds miss.

explanation.concept: Every production AI system needs a disable path that one on-call person can execute alone, without code review, deployment, or another team's approval — and that is exercised on a schedule. Automated breakers catch the failures metrics can see; the human path exists for the ones they cannot.
explanation.tip: When a stem says error rates were normal, it is ruling out every threshold-based answer. When it names the approvals required to flip a flag, the dependency chain is the finding.

topic: Handling a discrepancy between a supervisory return and the register
stem: A Swiss private bank's most recent supervisory return states that it operates four AI systems, none of which make customer-affecting decisions. The internal AI register now lists eleven entries, three of which describe systems that influence client-facing outcomes. The bank's own reporting standard requires every regulatory submission to be reconcilable to the source records that support it. A thematic supervisory review has just been announced. Which TWO actions should the head of compliance take? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Reconcile the return to the register: establish which of the eleven entries fell inside the return's stated definition and which did not, and document the definition that was applied when the return was prepared.
Reduce the register to the four systems named in the return, so that the bank's two records are consistent with one another before the review team begins its work.
Correct the submission through the bank's established amendment process if the reconciliation shows the return was wrong, rather than waiting for the review to identify the discrepancy.
Prepare a briefing note explaining the difference as a matter of interpretation, and hold it in reserve to present only if the review team raises the point directly.
Suspend the seven systems that were not covered by the return until the thematic review has concluded, so the submission is accurate as at the date of the review.

explanation.correct: The reconciliation has to come first because the discrepancy may not be an error at all — the return may have used a narrower definition that excluded seven entries legitimately, and until that is established nobody knows whether anything is wrong. What the standard requires is that the working be reproducible, so the definition applied must be written down. If the reconciliation does show the return was inaccurate, self-correction through the existing amendment route is the only defensible response: a supervisor who finds an error that the firm had already found and sat on treats it as a governance failure rather than a reporting one.

distractors.B: Editing the register to match the return destroys the source record in order to make the submission look supportable. It is the single most damaging action available here and would convert a reporting discrepancy into a conduct finding.
distractors.D: Preparing an explanation and disclosing it only if challenged makes candour contingent on detection. It also wastes the advantage the bank currently holds, which is that it found the discrepancy before the review team did.
distractors.E: Suspending seven running systems inflicts real business disruption to make a past submission retrospectively accurate, which it cannot do — the return described a period, not a date. It also looks like concealment rather than remediation.

explanation.concept: Regulatory reporting on AI is only as strong as the inventory beneath it and the definitions applied to it. Reconcile the submission to the source, record the definition used, and self-correct through the established route; never adjust the source record to fit the submission.
explanation.tip: When a stem mentions an internal standard requiring reconcilability, the first key is always the reconciliation. Options that change the source data rather than the report are traps you should rule out on sight.

topic: Purpose of separating AI approver from AI operator
stem: An AI governance standard requires that the person who approves a use case into production is not the same person who operates it. Which failure is that separation designed to prevent?

options.text: Knowledge of the system becoming concentrated in one person, so that its continued operation depends on that individual's availability.
The operating team being held responsible for outcomes that follow directly from decisions the approving body took.
One individual being able to widen what the system does without any independent party assessing the change.
Approval decisions being delayed because the person making them is simultaneously carrying a production workload.

explanation.correct: The scope of an AI system is unusually cheap to expand: a prompt edit, a new data source, an extra tool, a new user group. If the person who can make those changes is also the person who authorises them, the approval gate exists on paper only, because there is no moment at which anyone other than the operator has to be persuaded. Separation forces a second party to see the expansion. That is the specific failure being prevented — self-authorised scope creep, not resourcing or workload issues.

distractors.A: Key-person concentration is a real operational risk addressed through documentation, cross-training and rota design. Separation of duties does not help with it; if anything, splitting roles across people is orthogonal to whether either role is single-threaded.
distractors.B: Recording who decided what does clarify where responsibility sits, but that is a by-product. Separation exists to make the decision independent, not to protect the operating team from consequences flowing from it.
distractors.D: Throughput and reviewer capacity are governance design problems solved by tiering and delegation. Separation of duties adds a step rather than removing one, so speed cannot be its rationale.

explanation.concept: Separate the authority to change an AI system from the authority to approve the change. Without that split, scope expansion — more autonomy, more data, more users — happens with no independent assessment, and the approval record becomes a description of what the operator already decided.
explanation.tip: Separation-of-duties items nearly always resolve to self-authorisation. Discard options about availability, morale, or speed; they describe other controls.

topic: Acting on an aggregate pattern of unreported AI near-misses
stem: A Mexican utility runs a Claude assistant that answers field technicians' questions about equipment isolation procedures. Over eight weeks the support queue accumulated fourteen tickets whose text says the assistant gave an incorrect isolation procedure. Each was closed individually by an agent who corrected the technician; none was declared an incident, because in every case the technician caught it and no harm occurred. A safety engineer spots the pattern while reading ticket text for an unrelated review. The incident process has no mechanism that aggregates across tickets. What should the safety engineer do next?

options.text: Reopen the fourteen tickets and reclassify each as a low-severity AI incident, so that the volume appears correctly in the next monthly operational report.
Declare an incident against the aggregate pattern and let triage assess it, rather than leaving fourteen separately resolved tickets as the organisation's only record.
Raise a defect against the assistant's retrieval index, since incorrect isolation procedures point to stale or superseded procedure documents being returned.
Propose an amendment to the incident policy requiring any recurring AI-related ticket theme to be declared, and table it at the next governance forum.

explanation.correct: Fourteen wrong isolation procedures in eight weeks is not fourteen near-misses; it is one unresolved defect in a safety-critical instruction path that has been caught fourteen times by the last line of defence. The reason it never surfaced is that severity was assessed per event, and per event the harm was zero. Declaring against the pattern is what puts it in front of triage with the aggregate exposure visible, gets an owner assigned, and starts the clock. Everything else the engineer might sensibly do follows from that declaration rather than substituting for it.

distractors.A: Reclassifying closed tickets improves the statistics without mobilising anyone. Fourteen low-severity entries in a monthly report is precisely the presentation that caused the pattern to be overlooked in the first place.
distractors.C: Stale retrieval is a plausible cause and may well be right, but the engineer does not know that yet, and filing a defect commits the organisation to one hypothesis while bypassing triage. It also gets prioritised as ordinary engineering work rather than as a safety matter.
distractors.D: The policy gap is real and should be fixed. Taking it to a forum first means the live defect waits for a meeting, and the amendment would in any case be a postmortem action arising from the incident rather than a replacement for declaring it.

explanation.concept: Severity assessed per event systematically hides recurring defects that a human happens to catch each time. Build aggregation into the incident process — recurring themes, near-miss counts, repeated ticket text — and treat a pattern of caught errors as one incident, not as many resolved tickets.
explanation.tip: 'No harm occurred' in a stem is usually the reason nothing was declared, not the reason nothing should be. Next-step items reward containing the live risk over fixing the process that let it hide.

topic: Re-establishing ownership of an orphaned production AI system
stem: A Finnish media group built a Claude-based archive-tagging system with an external delivery partner. The partner's engagement ended, the internal team that sponsored the work was reorganised, and the register still names a product manager who left eight months ago. The system runs roughly 40,000 tagging calls a week and its output feeds the rights-clearance workflow that determines what the group may licence. Governance has flagged it. What must be established before anything else?

options.text: A support contract with the delivery partner covering defect fixes and model version upgrades for at least the next twelve months of operation.
A named accountable owner inside the current organisation with the authority and the budget to change, pause or retire the system.
A refreshed system card recording the current configuration, the evaluation results and the failure modes now known from production use.
Migration onto the group's standard AI platform so that the system falls under central monitoring, logging and cost attribution.

explanation.correct: Each of the other actions requires someone to commission it, fund it, and accept the result — and there is currently no such person. A system feeding rights clearance at this volume can produce a licensing error the group is answerable for, and today nobody in the organisation has standing to stop it. Establishing the owner is not a formality that precedes the real work; it is the thing that makes the real work assignable. Every remediation item beyond it is a decision that owner will make.

distractors.A: A support contract may be a sensible outcome, but nobody can sign or fund one without an owner, and it addresses defect fixes rather than the governance gap. It also deepens dependence on a partner who has already exited.
distractors.C: The card is genuinely missing and should be produced, but a document with no owner is a document nobody maintains. Refreshing it first produces an artefact that is accurate on the day it is written and stale within a quarter.
distractors.D: Platform migration improves observability and is a reasonable medium-term move. It is a substantial piece of engineering that requires a budget holder and an acceptance decision, neither of which exists until ownership is settled.

explanation.concept: An AI system with no accountable owner has no functioning governance, whatever documentation exists. When ownership is lost through reorganisation or partner exit, re-establishing a named owner with authority and budget is the first action; everything else is a decision for that owner.
explanation.tip: When a stem describes an orphaned system and offers several genuinely useful remediations, ask who would authorise each one. If the answer is nobody, the key is establishing ownership.

topic: Criteria that should drive an AI use case risk tier
stem: An Indian pharmaceutical company is designing a three-tier classification that routes AI use cases to light-touch, standard or full governance review. A working group has proposed candidate criteria for placing a use case into a tier. Which TWO criteria should determine the tier? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The severity and reversibility of the consequence if the output is wrong — a patient-facing or regulatory-submission error against an internal drafting error.
The model tier selected, on the basis that higher-capability models can perform a wider range of tasks and therefore carry more inherent risk into any deployment.
Whether the output is acted on without a competent human reviewing it first, since that determines whether an error reaches the world unfiltered.
The projected monthly token spend for the use case, which is the figure most consistently available and comparable across the proposals the group receives.
Whether the capability was built in-house or purchased, since purchased products have already passed through the supplying vendor's own assurance process.

explanation.correct: Risk is the product of how bad the outcome can be and how likely a bad output is to become that outcome. Severity and reversibility capture the first: a wrong sentence in an internal draft is recoverable, a wrong statement in a regulatory submission or to a patient may not be. The presence of a competent human between output and action captures the second: it is the difference between an error that gets caught and an error that lands. Together these two are sufficient to place almost any use case, and neither depends on implementation detail that will change.

distractors.B: Model capability is not a risk tier. A high-capability model summarising internal minutes is low risk; a cheap model deciding something patient-facing is not. Tiering on model choice also creates a perverse incentive to pick a weaker model to secure a lighter review.
distractors.D: Spend measures volume and cost, not exposure. A cheap, high-volume internal use can be low risk while a single expensive call inside a submission workflow is not, so a spend-based tier misclassifies in both directions.
distractors.E: Procurement route changes who performs assurance, not how much is needed. A purchased product still needs its own assessment, and vendor assurance covers the vendor's obligations rather than the buyer's use of the output.

explanation.concept: Tier AI use cases on consequence and autonomy: how severe and reversible the harm is if the output is wrong, and whether a competent human stands between the output and the action. Model, cost and build-versus-buy are implementation attributes, not risk drivers.
explanation.tip: In tiering items, reject any criterion the team can change without changing the exposure. If picking a cheaper model would move the tier, the criterion is wrong.

topic: Function of a compensating control in an AI exception
stem: An AI policy exception is granted because a required control cannot be implemented before a committed launch date. What is the purpose of the compensating control recorded alongside the exception?

options.text: To document the reasons the required control could not be implemented within the timescale that was available.
To transfer accountability for the exception from the approving body to the team that requested it.
To demonstrate to an auditor that the exception process was followed even though the outcome is non-compliant.
To bring the residual risk down to a level the approver is willing to carry for the life of the exception.

explanation.correct: An exception is a decision to run without a control, which leaves residual risk that somebody must consciously accept. The compensating control is what makes that acceptance defensible: a different mechanism, usually weaker or more manual, that covers enough of the same exposure for the remaining risk to be tolerable until the real control arrives. It changes the risk position rather than the paperwork, which is why an exception granted with no compensating control and no stated reason for its absence should not be granted at all.

distractors.A: The justification for the exception is a separate field and belongs in the request. Explaining why a control is absent does nothing to reduce the exposure that its absence creates.
distractors.B: Accountability for accepting risk sits with the approver and is not transferable by recording a control. If anything, granting an exception concentrates accountability on the approver rather than moving it away.
distractors.C: Audit evidence is an output of a functioning process, not its purpose. An exception with a compensating control that exists only on paper fails an audit precisely because the auditor tests whether it operates.

explanation.concept: An exception is a time-boxed risk acceptance. It needs four things: an owner, an expiry, a stated justification, and a compensating control that actually reduces residual risk for the duration. Missing the compensating control means the risk was accepted in full, whether or not anyone said so.
explanation.tip: Distinguish fields that describe the exception from the one that changes the risk. Only the compensating control does anything to the exposure itself.

topic: Changes that require re-issuing an approved system card
stem: A Portuguese hospital group's discharge-summary assistant has a system card approved fourteen months ago. The card names the model in use, lists the data sources the assistant retrieves from, records evaluation results on the group's own discharge cases, and describes the clinician sign-off step. The group's standard requires the card to be re-issued whenever a change makes something the card asserts no longer true. Which TWO of the following require re-issue? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Extending the retrieval corpus to include nursing notes, which were not previously reachable by the assistant.
Rerunning the evaluation suite against the unchanged configuration as part of the group's quarterly assurance cycle, with results inside the previously recorded range.
Upgrading to a newer model tier, with the evaluation suite rerun afterwards and the scores improving on every measure.
Correcting a formatting defect in the output template so that section headings render properly in the electronic patient record.
Confirming at the annual review that the clinician sign-off step is unchanged and continues to operate exactly as the card describes.

explanation.correct: The test the standard sets is narrow and mechanical: has a change made one of the card's assertions false? The card lists the data sources the assistant retrieves from, so adding nursing notes falsifies that list — and nursing notes carry clinical content the original evaluation never exercised. The card names the model and records evaluation results obtained on it, so a tier upgrade falsifies both, and the fact that scores improved is irrelevant to whether the card is accurate. Improvement is a reason to be pleased with the change, not a reason to leave a stale card in place.

distractors.B: Assurance testing that confirms the recorded results still hold is exactly what the card is for. Nothing it asserts has become untrue, and re-issuing on every assurance run would make version history meaningless.
distractors.D: A rendering fix in the output template changes presentation, not the tasks performed, the data reached, the behaviour evaluated, or the oversight step. None of the card's assertions is affected.
distractors.E: Confirming that a described control still operates is a validation of the card, not a change to it. The annual review record captures the confirmation; the card itself is unchanged because reality still matches it.

explanation.concept: A system card is a set of assertions about a specific deployment, and it must be re-issued whenever a change falsifies one — new data reachable, different model, different oversight, different approved task. Improvements trigger re-issue just as regressions do; the trigger is inaccuracy, not harm.
explanation.tip: Test each change against the card's contents rather than against your sense of how risky it is. A change that improves quality still invalidates a card that names the old model.

topic: Escalating an AI failure against an internal disclosure trigger
stem: A Korean online brokerage's Claude-based research summariser omitted a material risk disclosure from company summaries for eleven days; roughly 9,000 retail clients viewed an affected summary. The firm's internal standard states that any event which may have influenced a client investment decision is escalated to the disclosure committee within 24 hours of confirmation. The failure was confirmed this morning. The head of engineering notes that no client has complained and no affected trade has been identified, and proposes escalating once the impact analysis is finished next week. What is the correct course?

options.text: Complete the impact analysis first, so that the committee receives a quantified view of how many clients were affected rather than being asked to decide on visibly incomplete information.
Escalate only if a client complains or an affected trade is identified, since the standard is concerned with actual detriment rather than theoretical exposure.
Disclose directly to affected clients and to the regulator immediately, bypassing the committee, because any delay compounds the original failure.
Escalate to the disclosure committee now: the trigger is possible influence on a client decision and that is already confirmed, with the analysis supplied to the committee as it develops.

explanation.correct: The standard's trigger is written as 'may have influenced' and the clock starts at confirmation, not at quantification — the firm deliberately set a low, early threshold so that the disclosure judgement is made by the committee rather than by whoever is closest to the failure. Both conditions are already met: summaries seen by 9,000 clients omitted a material risk disclosure, and the failure was confirmed this morning. Waiting for the analysis substitutes engineering's assessment of materiality for the committee's, which is exactly the decision the standard removes from engineering.

distractors.A: Committees are constituted to decide under uncertainty and can be given analysis as it matures. Holding escalation until the picture is complete breaches a 24-hour trigger on the reasoning that the breach produces a better paper, and it hands the materiality judgement to the wrong party.
distractors.B: Absence of complaints is not evidence of absence of harm, particularly for an omission — a client who acted on an incomplete summary has no way of knowing something was missing. The standard was written in terms of possible influence precisely to avoid this inference.
distractors.C: Escalating past the accountable body is a governance failure in the opposite direction. The committee exists to decide what is disclosed, to whom, and when; an engineering lead making that call unilaterally creates a second incident.

explanation.concept: Escalation triggers are written to fire on suspicion and confirmation of the event, not on quantified impact. When a stem quotes a trigger, apply it literally: the point of a low threshold is that the people closest to the failure do not get to decide whether it is serious enough.
explanation.tip: Look for the exact wording of the internal trigger in the stem. 'May have' plus 'within 24 hours of confirmation' resolves the item on its own, before any argument about impact.

topic: Why AI risk challenge must report outside delivery
stem: Why should the function that reviews and challenges AI risk assessments report through a line separate from the function that builds and runs AI systems?

options.text: So that reviewers have the technical depth required to evaluate model and architecture choices on their own terms.
So that the cost of the review function can be carried centrally rather than charged against individual project budgets.
So that a challenge to a delivery decision cannot be overruled by the person whose delivery timeline the challenge affects.
So that regulators and auditors have a single named contact point for questions about the organisation's AI estate.

explanation.correct: Independence is about who can overrule whom. A reviewer whose objectives, performance rating and headcount sit under the executive responsible for shipping is structurally unable to hold a launch, because the person they would be blocking signs off their year. Separate reporting means a challenge that survives on its merits has somewhere to go, and it means the escalation path leads to a forum where delivery pressure and risk appetite are weighed by someone accountable for both.

distractors.A: Technical depth is a hiring and training question, and it is entirely achievable inside a delivery organisation. Some of the most technically capable reviewers sit in engineering; their problem is authority, not knowledge.
distractors.B: How review is funded affects behaviour at the margin, and project-charged review does create pressure to be brief. It is a budgeting arrangement rather than the structural reason independence exists.
distractors.D: A single external contact point is a coordination convenience and can be provided by any function, including one embedded in delivery. It says nothing about whether internal challenge can withstand pressure.

explanation.concept: A challenge function is only as independent as its reporting line. If the people who can overrule the reviewer also own the delivery date, the review is advisory whatever the policy calls it. Independence is structural, not a matter of the reviewer's seniority or intent.
explanation.tip: Independence questions resolve to authority, not expertise. Rule out options about skills, funding and external contact — they describe useful properties that do not require separation.

topic: A retired AI system still running against live credentials
stem: An Emirati port operator retired a Claude-based berth-planning pilot nine months ago and marked its register entry 'retired'. A scheduled reconciliation has now found the pilot's gateway credential still active, carrying low but non-zero traffic originating from a scheduled job inside a business unit's automation account. The team that sponsored the pilot was disbanded at the same time it was retired. Which conclusion is best supported, and should drive the remediation?

options.text: Decommissioning is recorded as a register status change with no corresponding technical action, so 'retired' in the register carries no assurance that a system has actually stopped.
The reconciliation cadence is too slow; had reconciliation run monthly instead of on the current cycle, the live credential would have been detected far earlier.

Business unit automation accounts should not be permitted to hold gateway credentials at all, and this account should be removed from the gateway's issuing scope with its workloads moved to platform-managed identities.
The register lacks a field for recording a system's technical dependencies, which is why the scheduled job was never identified when the pilot was retired.

explanation.correct: The register said retired and the system was running, which means the retirement process produced a status change and nothing else. That matters beyond this one credential: every other entry marked retired carries the same unverified claim, so the operator does not know how much of its supposedly decommissioned estate is still live, still holding access, and still without an owner since the sponsoring team was disbanded. The remediation is to make decommissioning a checklist with technical steps — credential revoked, jobs disabled, access removed — evidenced before the status can be set.

distractors.B: Faster reconciliation shortens the detection window, and the operator should probably run it more often. It treats the symptom: the credential would still have been left live, and every retirement would still depend on a later sweep to catch it.
distractors.C: Banning automation accounts from holding credentials would break legitimate scheduled workloads and is a heavy response to one stale job. The problem is not who held the credential but that nobody revoked it when the system was retired.
distractors.D: A dependencies field would help someone doing a careful retirement, but the evidence points to no technical retirement steps being performed at all. Adding a field to a process that is not executed does not change the outcome.

explanation.concept: Decommissioning must be an evidenced technical procedure — credentials revoked, scheduled jobs disabled, integrations removed — with the register status set only after those steps are confirmed. A lifecycle status that anyone can set by editing a field records intent, not reality.
explanation.tip: When the record and the system disagree, ask what the record was based on. If setting a status requires no evidence, every instance of that status across the estate is suspect, not just the one found.

topic: AI capability arriving inside an already-licensed SaaS product
stem: An Austrian retailer licenses a recruitment platform that it assessed and approved three years ago. The vendor has just announced a candidate-summarisation feature, enabled by default for all tenants at the next release, with no change to the contract or the commercial terms. The retailer's AI policy requires any AI system processing personnel data to be registered and assessed before use. The HR director's position is that nothing has been procured, so there is nothing to register. Which analysis is correct?

options.text: The policy applies: a new AI capability will process personnel data on the retailer's behalf, so it requires registration and assessment regardless of whether a separate purchase took place.
The policy does not apply, because the feature ships inside a product already assessed and approved; re-assessing on every vendor feature release would make the policy unworkable at scale.
The policy applies only once HR actually uses the feature, since no personnel data is processed until someone asks for a candidate summary to be generated.
The policy is the wrong instrument here; this is a change-management matter for the platform's service owner and should follow the retailer's standard vendor release process.

explanation.correct: The policy is written in terms of what happens to data, not in terms of how a capability was acquired. A default-on feature that summarises candidates will process personnel data whether or not money changed hands, and the original assessment three years ago examined a product that did not do this. The procurement framing is the trap: it makes registration contingent on a purchase order, which is exactly the gap through which embedded AI enters an organisation invisibly. Practically, the retailer needs to register the use, assess it, and decide before the release whether to leave it enabled.

distractors.B: The prior assessment covered prior behaviour. Treating an approval as permanent regardless of what the product later does converts a control into a one-off formality, and the workability objection is answered by tiering the re-assessment, not by skipping it.
distractors.C: Waiting for first use means the assessment happens after processing has begun, and with a default-on feature nobody will notice the moment it starts. The policy's word is 'before use', which requires acting at the release, not after it.
distractors.D: Vendor release management and AI assessment answer different questions. Release processes check compatibility, availability and rollout; they do not examine data reuse, model behaviour, or whether candidate summarisation is an acceptable input to a hiring decision.

explanation.concept: AI usage policy must be scoped by what processes data, not by what was purchased. The fastest-growing category of ungoverned AI is capability switched on inside products an organisation already owns, so registration triggers should include vendor feature releases, not only new procurements.
explanation.tip: When a stem stresses that no purchase occurred and no contract changed, that is the misdirection. Ask what will process which data, and apply the policy's own wording to that.

topic: Event that triggers off-cycle AI vendor re-assessment
stem: Outside the normal periodic review cycle, which event should trigger a re-assessment of a third-party AI product already in use?

options.text: The vendor publishes an updated independent security attestation covering the same scope as the previous one.
The vendor redesigns the product's user interface and navigation, so the organisation must reissue its user guidance and retrain staff.
The vendor changes the model or the model provider behind the product, or extends what the product does with customer data.
The organisation's usage grows past the volume band assumed in the vendor's original commercial proposal.

explanation.correct: Re-assessment is warranted when something changes that the original assessment's conclusions depended on. Two things do that for an AI product: the model or provider underneath it, which changes behaviour and the subprocessor chain your data flows through; and the scope of what the product does with your data, which changes the exposure being assessed. Neither is visible in your own change management, because neither requires you to deploy anything — which is why they have to be contractual notification triggers rather than things you hope to notice.

distractors.A: A refreshed attestation over unchanged scope is the vendor confirming that the position you already assessed still holds. It is evidence to file against the existing assessment, and its absence would be far more interesting than its arrival.
distractors.B: Interface changes affect usability and training. They do not alter what the product does with data or how it produces its output, so nothing in the risk assessment's reasoning is disturbed.
distractors.D: Volume growth is a commercial and capacity matter. It may warrant renegotiation and a look at rate limits, but the risk per transaction is unchanged, and tier or scope has not moved.

explanation.concept: Off-cycle vendor re-assessment should be triggered by changes to the underlying model or provider, to how your data may be used, or to the scope of the product's function. Write those as contractual notification obligations, because you cannot detect them from your own side.
explanation.tip: Ask which option changes a premise the original assessment relied on. Attestation renewals, interface refreshes and volume growth all leave the reasoning intact.

topic: Deciding notification of parties affected by an AI failure
stem: A Danish employment agency's Claude-based screening assistant applied an outdated eligibility rule for six weeks, causing about 300 applicants to be told they did not qualify for a training scheme they in fact qualified for. The incident is contained and the rule is corrected. The incident lead is preparing the notification decision. Which TWO points should govern how that decision is made? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The decision belongs to a named accountable executive advised by legal and communications, not to the incident lead or the engineering team who found the fault.
Notification should wait until the agency can confirm precisely which of the 300 applicants would have qualified, so that nobody is contacted unnecessarily.
The affected individuals need a remedy alongside the notice — a reopened application or a re-decision — because a notice without a route to correction transfers the burden onto them.
Because the error originated in a rule configuration rather than in the model's output, the agency should treat it as an ordinary process defect and use its standard service-correction letter.
Notification should be limited to applicants who have already contacted the agency to dispute their result, since the rest have shown no interest in the outcome.

explanation.correct: Two structural points govern this. First, deciding who gets told what is a decision with legal, reputational and regulatory consequence, so it sits with an accountable executive taking advice — not with the people running the technical response, who are neither positioned nor authorised to make it. Second, the notification is only meaningful if it comes with the thing the applicant actually needs: their application reopened and re-decided. A letter explaining that an automated system wrongly rejected someone, with no route to correction, converts the agency's error into the applicant's administrative task.

distractors.B: Perfect attribution before notification is a familiar way for a notification to never happen. Some of the 300 will not be resolvable from the records, and the applicants who were affected have a live interest in knowing now rather than at the end of a reconstruction exercise.
distractors.D: The origin of the fault does not determine what is owed to the people it harmed. Routing an automated adverse decision through a standard service-correction letter understates it and skips the question of whether the decision itself must be retaken.
distractors.E: Restricting notice to complainants makes the remedy available only to the most persistent, and the applicants least likely to challenge an automated rejection are frequently those with the least capacity to. It is a selection effect, not a scoping principle.

explanation.concept: Notification after an AI failure is an accountable-executive decision, not a technical one, and it must be paired with a remedy the affected person can use without further effort. Waiting for perfect attribution and limiting notice to those who complained are the two most common ways it degrades.
explanation.tip: Separate who decides from what the decision must contain — well-built multi-select items in this area key one of each. Options that narrow the affected population are almost always distractors.

topic: Composition of an AI approval board and missing ownership
stem: A Belgian rail operator's AI approval board consists of the CTO, the head of data, an enterprise architect and a procurement lead. It has approved thirty-one use cases in eighteen months. An external review examined the four cases where harm later materialised — all of them customer-facing decisions about compensation for delayed journeys — and found that the board minutes for those four contain detailed discussion of data flows, model choice and supplier terms, but no discussion at all of what happens to a passenger when the system gets it wrong. What change to the board addresses the root cause?

options.text: Require the requesting team to submit a written risk assessment ahead of each meeting so the board reviews prepared analysis rather than reacting to a presentation given on the day.
Appoint an external adviser with AI ethics expertise as a standing member to provide independent challenge on the societal impact of the proposals the internal members are close to.
Rotate board membership on an annual cycle so that a wider range of functional perspectives is brought to bear on approval decisions over time.
Add the accountable owner of the affected business process — passenger services — as a standing member with a decision right, so the consequence has an owner in the room.

explanation.correct: The board's composition explains its blind spot exactly. Four technology and supply functions produced minutes rich in data flows, model choice and supplier terms, because those are the questions its members own. Nobody present owned the passenger, so nobody asked what a wrong compensation decision does to one. Adding the business owner with a decision right, rather than as an invited observer, means the consequence is represented by someone who carries it and who can decline to accept a proposal. A board reviews what its members are accountable for; change the accountability in the room and the minutes change with it.

distractors.A: Better inputs do not create new questions. A written assessment prepared by the requesting team and read by the same four functions would emphasise the same dimensions, and the review found the discussion was detailed rather than rushed.
distractors.B: An ethics adviser adds a perspective but not accountability, and advisory voices in a technology-dominated board are routinely noted and moved past. The gap here is the absence of the person who owns the outcome, not the absence of an outside opinion.
distractors.C: Rotation varies who attends across years without guaranteeing that the affected business is ever represented, and it costs the board continuity of judgement. It is a diversity mechanism applied to an accountability problem.

explanation.concept: An approval body examines what its members are accountable for. Whenever an AI decision affects a customer or a business process, the owner of that process needs a seat with a decision right — otherwise the board scrutinises the build thoroughly and the consequence not at all.
explanation.tip: When a stem tells you what the minutes did and did not contain, map that against the job titles listed. The missing topic almost always matches a missing role.

topic: First move after confirming a confidential-data shadow AI leak
stem: A Czech engineering consultancy's egress logs show that a project team has spent eight months sending structural calculation notes to a consumer AI product from personal accounts on company laptops. The notes contain a client's unpublished design drawings held under a non-disclosure agreement. Access to the service was blocked at the proxy this morning as soon as the logs were reviewed, and the team has been told to stop. The AI governance lead has just been handed the evidence. What is the next step?

options.text: Report the confidentiality exposure to the client straight away, since the non-disclosure agreement has been breached and delay worsens the consultancy's position.
Establish the scope — what data left, over what period, to which service, and under which account terms — before any notification or enforcement decision is taken.
Extend the proxy block to every consumer AI service and revoke local administrator rights across the consultancy, so that no comparable route remains open to anyone.
Register the use in the AI inventory and put it through the standard assessment so that it becomes a governed use case on the sanctioned platform.

explanation.correct: The immediate exposure is already contained — the proxy block is in place and the team has stopped — so nothing is gained by acting before the facts are known. Everything that comes next depends on scope: whether the client must be told, and what they must be told, depends on which drawings left and when; whether personal accounts were used under consumer terms determines what rights the provider has over the content; and any enforcement action needs a defensible account of what actually happened. Notifying or disciplining on a partial picture usually has to be corrected later, which is worse than a short, deliberate delay.

distractors.A: Client notification is very likely required and should not be delayed unreasonably, but a notification that cannot say which drawings were exposed or over what period forces a second conversation and undermines confidence in the consultancy's control of its own systems.
distractors.C: Blanket blocking and estate-wide rights revocation is a large, disruptive change made in the first hour of an investigation. The specific route is already closed; broad hardening is a remediation decision that belongs after scoping and with the affected business consulted.
distractors.D: Registering the use presumes an outcome. Whether structural calculations under a client NDA should be processed by any AI service is precisely the question the assessment would answer, and it cannot be decided before the extent of what has already happened is known.

explanation.concept: Once a shadow AI exposure is contained, scoping precedes notification, remediation and enforcement. Establish what data left, over what period, to which service, and under which terms — every subsequent decision is a function of those four facts.
explanation.tip: Check whether the stem has already contained the exposure. If it has, options that contain it further are no longer the next step, however sensible they read.
